articles.title: Catherine's emotional cancer documentary strips away the stiff upper lip
articles.summary: The Princess of Wales has made a documentary, Heal, describing her cancer experience in her own words.
articles.body:
The Princess of Wales's personal account of her experience of cancer has a soul-bearing, emotionally candid tone never presented before in a royal documentary.

Discussing it at a private screening, she said it reflected the "fear, anxiety, uncertainty" shared by hundreds of thousands of people each year "who receive the words no one wants to hear" about having cancer.

The documentary, Heal, being shown on BBC One on Sunday, couldn't be further away from a stiff upper lip.

This is royal television without any palaces or carriages, it's an intense 30 minutes examining how "cancer strips everything away" and then a different kind of self-awareness emerges.

It reveals more of Catherine's inner thoughts than any of her previous speeches and we hear more from her children than ever before.

"Cancer does change you. It changes your body, it changes you physically. You have to go through treatment and surgeries and everything.

"But there's a much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you. I think when you've had to confront your own vulnerabilities, you know, when you're faced with your own mortality, you have to accept that life is not infinite and in those moments, yes, a shift does happen," she says.

'An emotional directness that's an unusual departure'

Some viewers might be left in tears, others may think it's too schmaltzy - either way, they're going to be talking about it. It packs an emotional punch, even though it's more of a self-scripted, video diary than a conventional, journalistic documentary.

"This will be a documentary that most people can relate to and will admire her for doing. There is an emotional directness that's an unusual departure," says royal commentator Prof Pauline MacLaran, of Royal Holloway, University of London.

MacLaran thinks it will connect well with the public, who will admire Catherine's "bravery".

The documentary follows Catherine's Three Peaks Challenge, in which she climbed the biggest mountains in England, Wales and Scotland in a single day, and the cameras record her driving in between and her encounters with other climbers.

This climb is a big mountainous metaphor for the difficulties, resilience and help of other people during the "scary, disorientating experience" of her treatment.

At the summit of one peak she gets voice messages from her three children - George, Louis and Charlotte - who each in turn send their love in a way that shows the closeness of their family. They also all hug and kiss later, along with Prince William, with tears being brushed away.

Those moments could be the emotional peaks that people will share, in a documentary made for the social media age.

It's also probably the most we've heard directly from the royal children.

Somewhere, the late Prince Philip will be scratching his head at how much the royals have dropped their tradition of privacy. Although we don't learn from the film the type of cancer or any details of Catherine's treatment.

"No previous generation of the Royal Family would have considered producing something like this," says Valentine Low, author and royal commentator.

"They would have been less willing to talk about illness and personal matters," he says.

But this documentary is in keeping, says Low, with a generation "that's more likely to think in terms of whether there could be a positive message from the experience".

'Giving back' to people facing similar health worries

Nonetheless, says Low, such a film-making approach, sharing their own chosen thoughts with the camera without an interviewer, still allows Catherine to "control the narrative".

And there are questions that arise. She speaks of her cancer journey being a "pilgrimage" and the need to "spend time on our spiritual health" - and it makes you wonder whether there has been a deeply religious or spiritual experience as part of her recovery.

There's a melancholy tone to the documentary, describing the impact of a "really dark time", and you wonder how this will sit alongside the expectations of her future royal life, when she will be queen.

It could also raise wider questions about the treatment, waiting times and recovery support available to the great majority of NHS patients, who do not have royal titles, but whose needs are as intense.

But we see Catherine in this documentary in hospital wards sharing experiences with other cancer patients and hearing about their hopes and fears. It's deliberately raw and unadorned in how it's presented.

There are lighter moments too, joking with her brother James as they head up the mountains.

Speaking at a screening, Catherine said the documentary was about "giving back" to people facing similar health worries and also to recognise the support of health services and charities working with patients and families.

Proceeds from the documentary, like her Three Peaks Challenge fundraiser, will go to the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, in support of the hospital where she received treatment.

The open, empathetic tone of the documentary has been warmly welcomed by those working with cancer patients.

"Watching someone speak so openly about the fear, the hope and the long road to recovery can make a real difference to those going through it," says Michelle Mitchell, chief executive of Cancer Research UK.

"Her honesty will help many people feel less alone, and it will encourage important conversations about cancer in homes across the country."

Ceinwen Giles, co-chief executive of Shine Cancer Support, said: "The film's honesty is what makes it so powerful.

"By being open about her experience, the princess gives others a way to start their own conversations about how cancer affects every part of a person's life, particularly younger adults and those with young families."

Catherine herself says that her experience has made her think about well-being in a much more holistic way, "not just about fixing what is wrong. It is about finding balance in how we live."

"My hope is that this film will encourage compassion, showing the real value in standing alongside one another in the hardest of times," she says.

Heal will be shown on BBC iPlayer from 12:00 GMT and BBC One at 18:40 GMT on 29 November. It will also air internationally, including on NBCUniversal in the US on 30 November, Channel 9 in Australia on 1 December and CTV and Noovo in Canada on 7 December

articles.title: 'Poison seller' Kenneth Law apologises in court to the families of his victims
articles.summary: The Canadian man, who pleaded guilty to 14 counts of aiding and abetting suicide earlier this year, said he was remorseful for his actions.
articles.body:
The Canadian man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries apologised in court to the families of the victims, saying he deeply regrets his actions and will never repeat them.

Kenneth Law made the remarks on Friday during a sentencing hearing where prosecutors asked a judge to give him a 25-year prison term.

The 61-year-old pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.

He will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.

During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.

If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.

As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people".

"What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said.

She also said Law's motives were financial.

"If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.

Law's defence lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, countered those claims, arguing that his client was not responsible for any of their battles with mental illness..

"Each of these incidents is its own unique tragedy," Gourlay said. "Mr Law may be a common denominator between them, but Mr Law was not the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all these victims to seek out his products in the first place."

He said Law held a "misguided belief" he was helping his victims

Law's defence attorney has asked the court to give him a 12-year sentence.

At the end of the hearing, Law told the court that he had deep regret for aiding in the suicide deaths of his victims.

"To the families of the victims, words can never replace the loss of your loved ones. I convey my deepest condolences. I remain remorseful. I'm sorry."

The sentencing hearing followed an emotional few days of testimony in September, when grieving family members and friends told the court of the pain Law had caused.

Those impact statements will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date.

Authorities said the former chef sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients - who he met in online suicide forums - in 40 countries, roughly a quarter of which were sent to the UK.

articles.title: NBC pulls controversial anti-Israel ad after igniting fury from Jewish groups
articles.summary: NBC pulled a controversial anti-Israel ad that aired during a primetime "Saturday Night Live" Thanksgiving special, sparking backlash among Jewish groups.
articles.body: NBC has pulled a controversial anti-Israel ad from its airwaves after sparking backlash over the Thanksgiving holiday, Fox News Digital has confirmed. During a Thanksgiving-themed "Saturday Night Live" primetime special Wednesday night, NBC aired an ad featuring a girl raising money for a $400 bike, juxtaposing her with a Palestinian girl with a missing leg standing on crutches in front of a pile of rubble. "Every three seconds, our government sends $400 of taxpayer money to Israel to do this," a narrator tells viewers while showing the injured Gazan child on screen. MS RACHEL CALLS SILENCE ON GAZA CONFLICT 'F---ED UP,' SAYS IT UPSETS HER SO MUCH SHE NOW SWEARS The 30-second ad, funded by the IMEU (Institute for Middle East Understanding) Policy Project, directs viewers to a website named No More For Israel, criticizing what it describes as the U.S. government's weapons "giveaway" to Israel and accusing the Jewish state of "committing a genocide" against Palestinians. The site urges Americans to pressure lawmakers to oppose any weapons deal with Israel. Jewish groups and pro-Israel advocates criticized the ad as antisemitic, with many pointing out that the ad makes no mention that the ongoing conflict in Gaza began with the Oct. 7 terrorist attack committed by Hamas against Israel. MANDANI GRILLED ON RHETORIC TOWARD OCT 7, COMBATTING ANTISEMITISM AS JEWISH NEW YORKERS FEAR CURRENT CLIMATE "NBC took money to tell millions of Americans that our support for Israel is responsible for the horrific injury of a Palestinian child," American Jewish Committee CEO Ted Deutch wrote on X. "Here’s what the ad leaves out: the vicious Hamas terrorists who launched this war on October 7 by slaughtering, raping, and kidnapping Israelis, dragging hostages into Gaza, and then fighting from among Palestinian civilians, with horrific consequences for Israelis and Gazans alike. "The suffering of Palestinian civilians is real and heartbreaking. But using that suffering to demonize Israel while writing Hamas out of the story isn’t an honest debate," the former Democratic congressman continued. "We can debate American policy and assistance to Israel. And yes, this was a paid advertisement. But 'we were paid to run it' cannot be the end of the discussion. Networks decide what they will and will not put on the air every day. NBC chose to take the money and run this ad. "It should explain why and how an ad this one-sided and manipulative met its standards for what it will put on the air. And if this meets NBC’s standards, Americans deserve to know what those standards are." The Israeli-American Council (IAC) characterized the ad as a clear example of "antisemitic blood libel aimed at denying the Jewish state its right to defend itself against terrorists and murderers." "Words and images have consequences," the group shared in a statement to Fox News Digital. "They can normalize antisemitic hatred, embolden people to act on it and endanger innocent lives." The IAC called on NBC to "come clean about how this advertisement met its own standards and ensure it is not aired again." Anti-Defamation League CEO Jonathan Greenblatt also slammed NBC's decision to air the ad. "Broadcasting an ad that blatantly demonizes the Jewish state and makes false claims about the use of American taxpayer dollars during primetime on the eve of a family holiday isn’t just insensitive. It’s indefensible," he wrote. "At a moment of escalating antisemitism, there is no rationale to justify fanning the flames with such a twisted narrative." UK ANTISEMITISM ADVISOR LAUNCHES PROBE INTO BBC, SAYS CULTURE DEMANDS JEWISH STAFFERS 'JUSTIFY' EXISTENCE "Modern day Nazi propaganda compliments of NBC. Every person who approved this ad buy should be identified and terminated," the advocacy group Stop Antisemitism wrote. A source familiar with the matter told Fox News Digital that senior leadership at NBC was unaware of the ad until after it aired and that the network intends to reevaluate its ad review process going forward. articles.body: An anonymous donor walked into a bank in Ohio and paid off the remaining $104,000 mortgage on a homeless shelter, leaving its staff stunned by the unexpected gesture. The surprise came to light in October 2024 when the treasurer of Geauga Faith Rescue Mission noticed an unusual transaction in the organisation's financial records and contacted executive director Nathan Long. After checking the account, Long discovered that the mortgage had been cleared by someone who had visited another branch of the bank. The donor later sent the shelter a letter explaining the gesture and requesting anonymity. In the message, the individual offered a simple reminder: "There's still a lot of good in this world."An unexpected bank transaction reveals a mystery benefactorThe incident came to light after the shelter's board treasurer noticed an unusual payment of approximately $102,000 in its financial records. Long initially had no explanation for the transaction and decided to investigate it.He subsequently visited the bank, where he learnt that an unidentified individual had gone to another branch and paid off the remaining mortgage balance directly. The donor also sent the organisation a letter explaining the contribution and asking not to be identified publicly.According to reports by Cleveland 19 News and News 5 Cleveland, the individual wanted the shelter to continue its work and reminded its staff that good people still existed despite difficult circumstances.The organisation was left with a fully paid-off property and one less major financial obligation.Shelter had been helping homeless men since 2022Geauga Faith Rescue Mission is a faith-based nonprofit organisation established in October 2014 by Mike Farrell, whose childhood experience with homelessness inspired him to help people facing similar circumstances.The organisation initially operated a voucher programme before opening its first emergency men's shelter at 339 Washington Street in Chardon on November 13, 2022.The facility provides temporary accommodation, meals, spiritual guidance and support to men experiencing homelessness in Geauga County. Its work is aimed at helping residents access essential services and move towards more stable living arrangements.At the time of the donation, the shelter was accommodating men who needed emergency housing and support while facing difficult personal and financial circumstances.Anonymous donation supported plans for a women's shelterThe mortgage payment also came at a time when the organisation was working to expand its services to women experiencing homelessness.Geauga Faith Rescue Mission had identified a need for a separate emergency shelter for women in the county. articles.title: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
articles.summary: China's immense clout now also has the flex of soft power. Critics and dissidents say their voices are being drowned out.
articles.body:
For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar.

"Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500."

It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang. Beijing, which said the camps were for "re-education" to counter separatist violence, denied the allegations detailing alarming rights abuses.

But an international outcry, including protests, followed. Western governments rolled out trade bans and sanctions against senior Chinese officials, and froze their assets, and at least nine countries issued parliamentary resolutions condemning the detentions.

It was a time "when we felt the world was finally listening", says Dolkun, 59, who served as president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress from 2017-2024 .

But today, "we find ourselves competing against economic interests and geopolitical calculations to capture the world's attention. For me, this is one of the most painful aspects of our struggle".

Few corners of the world remain untouched by China's rise. Its electric vehicles pack highways from Brazil to Belgium, made-in-China batteries, solar panels, AI models and microdramas fuel daily consumption in so many places, and Labubu dolls , Pop Mart's furry gap-toothed plush, dangle from backpacks almost everywhere.

China's immense economic clout now also has the flex of soft power , drowning out voices that say their fight against the Communist Party cannot compete with the country's gleaming skylines, advanced exports or futuristic ambitions.

Buoyed by its successes, Beijing is also swapping the "stick" for the "carrot", says Uyghur journalist Arslan Hidayat, who was born and raised in Australia, where he runs Kashgar Times.

Activists tell the BBC Beijing has been offering family reunions, money and the promise of safety - in return, they are asked for information about their networks and to promote pro-party narratives. The result, activists say, is a movement with fewer voices and less trust.

The Chinese embassy in the UK dismissed the activists' claims that they would be asked to spy on or disclose information about fellow exiles.

China's "economic muscle" has earned it respect abroad and reshaped foreign policy, says Ian Johnson, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who has long reported on Chinese civil society.

"At the same time, Western governments have become much more inwardly focused and populist, pushing human rights down their lists of priorities."

China's human rights record has not earned a mention in any of the three summits Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump held this year, including the one in Shenzhen last week. As Beijing's leverage on the global stage has grown, so has the cost of confrontation or condemnation.

This shift in Beijing's image and tactics is deeply worrying, dissidents say, because it is weakening both their networks and the international pressure they hope to build.

In July Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen died after he set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in New York. He was protesting against China's sweeping new "ethnic unity law" which, among other things, requires minorities, including Tibetans, to learn Mandarin. The UN called it an "absolutely tragic" incident, but attention quickly faded.

His death was "an appeal to the international community", says Tenzin Dorjee, a researcher at the Tibet Action Institute, but he thinks much of the world is reluctant to criticise China because of the power it wields.

That same month Dolkun tried to rally supporters against the same law but he met with a muted response.

"Many people have dialled down on their activism over the years because they are thinking about their loved ones back in China," Dolkun says.

Arslan says he has interviewed at least a dozen Uyghur exiles who were "invited to go back to China on the condition that they would provide information to Chinese agents from time to time".

The questions seem "fairly innocuous", he adds: "Who lives around you? Which Uyghur restaurants do you frequent? We believe these are used to build out the profiles of dissidents overseas."

Beijing's embassy in the UK said in its response to the BBC that "facilitating visits to China by overseas Chinese to reunite with their families" is a "normal part" of consular services.

"China respects and protects the lawful rights and interests of people of all ethnic groups, including the Uyghurs, and their freedom to maintain contact with family members overseas," it added.

These family visits often happen in large groups and are well documented on China's official platforms.

In Turkey, which hosts tens of thousands of Muslim minorities from Xinjiang, Chinese Consul-General Wei Xiaodong was photographed sending off some 30 participants from Istanbul in January.

"He expressed hope that the diaspora returning to Xinjiang would experience the region's development... and would actively promote these developments upon their return to Turkey," read a post on the consulate's WeChat page.

Beijing has repackaged Xinjiang into a traveller's haven. The region saw more than 300 million domestic and international tourist visits last year, more than double the number in 2018, Chinese authorities say.

The post from China's Turkish consulate concluded with a clip showing loved ones hugging and presenting bouquets as they reunite with family at the airport in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang.

"People are happy to stay quiet and lay low for the little communication they've been allowed to establish with their loved ones," Arslan says.

Though the trips are publicised, it is unclear what makes someone eligible to participate in them. Some suggest that even dating histories come under the microscope.

Alim*, a Uyghur exiled in Turkey, says a friend who made an appeal to the consulate to consider her for a trip was rejected, with staffers alluding to her past relationship with a Kazakh man who at one point was "quite active" in lobbying for his parents who were detained in China.

"She was very eager to go on one of these 'family visits' because she hasn't seen her loved ones back home in so many years... She was crushed that she was rejected," says Alim.

"The way I understand it, the 'ideal participant' is someone influential enough to amplify China's messages, yet not associated with anything or anyone too political."

When Mehmut* was invited on a family visit in October 2024, he jumped at the opportunity.

The Uyghur businessman hoped a trip back to China would help him re-establish the links needed to "keep our business afloat". Far from the warm reunions Mehmut had expected, he says his engagement with friends and family "felt superficial".

"It was not like officials were actively monitoring me or restricting my movements. But there was a great dose of fear and self-censorship in my conversations with people," he says.

"Some were caught off guard to see me return, others appeared very cautious with what they told me. The experience just made me feel very uncomfortable."

These visits do not just serve Beijing's narrative; they also drive a wedge within communities, activists say.

Abduweli Ayup, a prominent Uyghur linguist based in Norway, has observed former activists going off the grid after returning from these trips.

"Some have deleted their social media accounts and cut off contact with us," he says. "Others appear to be suspicious of us or concerned that what we were doing would compromise theirs or their families' safety."

The fact that only a few get selected to visit the homeland "creates confusion within the diaspora," says Tibetan activist Karma Rinchen.

"They get sidelined when they return... Very sadly, our suspicions that some of them are feeding information back to the Chinese authorities have turned out to be true."

Rinchen serves as information secretary in the Tibetan government-in-exile in the northern Indian town of Dharamshala. His parents were among thousands who followed their spiritual leader Dalai Lama into exile after China annexed Tibet.

Over the decades, waves of others have fled Chinese rule seeking greater freedom or asylum from Beijing's crackdowns - dissidents and student activists in the wake of the Tiannanmen Square massacre; lawyers, journalists, purged officials and critics in the years after, and, more recently, Hong Kong saw a steady exodus build as the pro-democracy movement was crushed.

Many have kept on fighting. But now, they say, Beijing's might is chipping away at their struggle, making it ever harder to stand up to the Chinese Communist Party.

"Many among us have been separated from our families for generations and are eager to set foot on Tibet soil," Rinchen says. "This is exactly the kind of desperation the Communist Party seeks to target."

But he adds this only means communities have to "work harder to make sure their voices are heard".

"For Tibetans, this is not something we can simply walk away from. Our struggle is about our identity, our culture, our religion and the basic rights of our people. We have been doing this work for many decades, and we have learned to remain patient and persistent," Rinchen adds.

For many, that persistence continues to be tested on a personal level.

Uyghur musician Mirkamel Tourghoun has lived as a refugee in Paris since 2008, spending most of his time writing music and making films about Uyghur culture.

The 42-year-old has chosen the painful path of cutting off contact with his family who remain in Urumqi.

In January, he received a call from someone claiming to be an official from the city.

"What if we get rid of all this [political] pressure, and allow you to return and see your parents? Do you have such plans?" the caller asked.

"What's happened in the past is in the past. You should turn a new page. The pen is in your own hand."

The official claimed his father was gravely ill and that time was running out to see him. "It's emotional blackmail," Mirkamel says.

He declined the official's invitation: "Tell my family to forget they ever had a child like me. There is no other solution."

articles.title: Scotland has released 50 wildcats into the Highlands since 2023, with females giving birth in the wild for three consecutive years as efforts to restore the species' population continue
articles.summary: Scotland’s efforts to bring its critically endangered wildcats back from the brink have reached an important milestone, with 50 animals released into the
articles.body: Scotland’s efforts to bring its critically endangered wildcats back from the brink have reached an important milestone, with 50 animals released into the Highlands since 2023. The conservation programme has also recorded a promising sign of recovery, as female wildcats have given birth in the wild for three consecutive years. More than 44 kittens have been born since the project began, suggesting that the released animals are not only adapting to their natural surroundings but are also beginning to establish a breeding population in the Cairngorms.50 wildcat releases are helping restore Scotland’s native populationThe milestone was announced by Saving Wildcats, a conservation partnership led by the Royal Zoological Society of Scotland (RZSS). The programme began releasing wildcats into the Cairngorms National Park in summer 2023, with the aim of preventing the species from disappearing from Scotland.The latest milestone was reached after 4 additional wildcats were released during the summer of 2026. According to RZSS and the Saving Wildcats project, the total number of animals released has now reached 50 in 4 years.The programme's progress is particularly significant because Scottish wildcats have faced decades of decline. The animals were once found across mainland Britain but suffered from persecution, habitat pressures and interbreeding with domestic and feral cats.According to STV News, the species was declared functionally extinct in 2019. The conservation programme is now working to rebuild a population that can survive and reproduce without depending entirely on continued releases.What makes the birth of wild kittens an important sign of recoveryOne of the most encouraging developments has been the arrival of kittens born in their natural habitat. Saving Wildcats confirmed that female wildcats have given birth in the wild for three consecutive years, indicating that the released animals are adjusting to life outside captivity.STV News reported that more than 44 kittens had been born in the wild since the programme began. This is an important development because successful reproduction suggests that the animals are finding suitable conditions, surviving in their surroundings and continuing their population in the wild.David Barclay, conservation manager at Saving Wildcats, told STV News that the animals were not simply surviving, hunting and living independently but were also reproducing.How are the released wildcats being monitoredReleasing animals into a large natural landscape is only one part of the conservation work. The team also needs to understand how they move, hunt and adapt after leaving the breeding centre.According to STV News, every wildcat released through the programme is fitted with a GPS collar. These devices allow conservationists to follow the animals' movements and collect information about their behaviour after they enter the wild.David Barclay explained that tracking provides an important way to understand how the animals are adapting. The information is also reviewed and shared with other conservation projects, allowing researchers to learn from both successful outcomes and difficulties.The animals are bred and prepared at a dedicated conservation breeding centre at Highland Wildlife Park before being released into the Cairngorms. Preparing a wildcat for release takes around 15 months.During this period, human contact is deliberately kept to a minimum. The approach helps prevent the animals from becoming accustomed to people and reduces the likelihood of them approaching humans in search of food once they are living independently.STV News also reported that some released wildcats have already been spotted by members of the public. One particularly unusual sighting involved a wildcat swimming across the River Spey while people were canoeing nearby.Threats facing the Scottish wildcatsDespite the encouraging breeding results, conservationists have warned that the species remains critically endangered in Scotland. Several threats continue to affect its chances of long-term survival.One of the biggest concerns is hybridisation, which happens when wildcats breed with domestic or feral cats. This can gradually weaken the distinct genetic identity of Scotland's native wildcat population.Other threats include feline diseases, road collisions, accidental harm from predator control activities and the fragmentation of suitable habitats. Human activity can also disturb areas where wildcats live and hunt.The Saving Wildcats project recorded 11 deaths among released animals over 3 years, including 5 caused by vehicle collisions. However, the conservation team considers this mortality rate relatively successful compared with similar animal relocation projects.RZSS also noted that several of the animals that died had spent years living in the wild and produced litters before their deaths.Scotland plans to strengthen the population through further releasesNext priority is to increase the population while ensuring that it has enough genetic diversity to remain healthy over time.RZSS has said that future releases will include animals bred with Spanish wildcats, which are the closest living genetic relatives of Scotland's native wildcats. Introducing these animals is expected to help strengthen the genetic diversity of the population.Dr Helen Senn, head of conservation and science programmes at RZSS, warned that wildcats face additional pressures from climate change. Wildfires during the summer of 2026 caused extensive damage to known wildcat habitats in the Cairngorms National Park.The project also works with farmers, land managers and local communities because wildcat habitats frequently overlap with land used by people. These areas include forest edges, rough grassland, scrubland and riverside environments.Meanwhile, Scotland's new Wildcat Strategy, published by NatureScot in September 2026, builds on the experience gained through the Saving Wildcats programme. As reported by STV News, the strategy aims to tackle the biggest threats facing the species, identify additional safe release areas and restore wildcat numbers to sustainable levels by 2045.You use AI every day. articles.title: A clinic is reassessing people with ADHD and autism diagnoses - but critics fear it could deepen stigma
articles.summary: While many people find a diagnosis for ADHD or autism affirming, a government-funded clinic in Sweden is re-assessing people who feel it does not reflect them.
articles.body:
Freya looks nervous as she walks into a psychiatric clinic in Sweden for an ADHD assessment.

Countries around the world have seen a huge increase in ADHD diagnoses over recent decades. For many people this can be life changing, helping them understand themselves better and access support.

But Freya (not her real name) is not attending a long-awaited appointment to secure a diagnosis.

This government-funded clinic offers autism and ADHD diagnosis reassessments - its doctors believe it is the first in the world dedicated solely to this purpose.

At 12, Freya was struggling with anxiety at school and sought out professional help. "They thought I had ADHD," she says.

But as she grew up, she felt that she did not experience ADHD symptoms. "I don't think I had it in the first place," she now says.

Her doubts about the diagnosis became more pressing as a teenager, when she discovered that in Sweden, it could be a barrier to pursuing her dream career of joining the police.

"I want to have every option open," she tells BBC World Service.

If the doctors at the clinic decide Freya does not meet the ADHD criteria, her medical records will be updated, and it will be easier for her to apply for a job with the police.

The clinic, known as Mottagning Neuropsykiatri, has opened at a time when rates of ADHD and autism diagnoses are under the spotlight. Many say this is because of greater awareness of the symptoms, and that previously neglected groups - particularly women and girls - are finally getting the diagnoses they need, while others argue that the growing numbers stem from overdiagnosis.

The existence of the clinic is controversial. Clinical guidance from UK governing bodies and the World Health Organization describe autism as a lifelong condition and ADHD as a neurodevelopmental condition that can persist into adulthood. The medical consensus is that both diagnoses last a lifetime, even if symptoms fluctuate.

And some neurodiversity advocates warn that a dedicated reassessment service could reinforce the idea that being diagnosed with ADHD or autism is undesirable – and deepen the stigma surrounding both conditions.

Despite this, hundreds of people have approached the clinic about reassessment.

Like Freya, other young adults have been prompted to reconsider their diagnosis after they felt it had become a barrier.

This is because historically, Swedes with ADHD or autism were barred from certain jobs, including joining the military, and becoming police officers, train drivers and pilots. This is despite research suggesting some neurodivergent traits can be strengths in certain roles. No such bans exist in the UK, although rules differ globally.

Since 2022, people with ADHD have been able to join the Swedish military if they are medication-free. And since 2021, people with ADHD or autism have been able to apply to join the police, but must submit a medical certificate, which can cost around 15,000 SEK (£1,100) privately.

When Freya was referred to the clinic, she says she was relieved to find out she could get her diagnosis reassessed there for free.

Johanna, 24, was diagnosed with ADHD at 14 after what she describes as a period of bad behaviour at school. She found the diagnosis helpful at first and received additional support from teachers.

But as she grew into adulthood, she says she stopped feeling that she needed extra support. And after discovering it was a barrier to becoming a police officer, she began questioning whether it was even accurate.

Johanna says she has some traits of ADHD, such as a short attention span, "but not enough to have an ADHD diagnosis," she believes.

Johanna was reassessed aged 21 during an early pilot of the reassessment clinic and was found not to meet its diagnostic criteria for ADHD. She now works for her father's company, and does not plan on becoming a police officer.

Both ADHD and autism are neurodevelopmental conditions that affect how people think and interact with the world. They are diagnosed through detailed assessments, which can include questionnaires and interviews, rather than one single clinical test.

The doctors at Mottagning Neuropsykiatri say their approach is different from traditional assessments, as it focuses less on someone's history, and more on the symptoms they are experiencing in the present.

"This is not de-diagnosing, this is a renewed assessment of your functioning today," says Sebastian Lundström, the clinic's lead psychologist.

The doctors say they do not judge whether the original assessment was correct, so rather than wiping the original diagnosis from patients' medical records, they add a note of the new assessment.

Lundström says that some people who once had a diagnosis but are found to not meet the criteria at the clinic may have been misdiagnosed. But he also believes that for a small minority, ADHD and autism are not lifelong conditions and individuals may stop experiencing symptoms as they grow older.

But updating a person's diagnosis because they are not currently showing symptoms is a contested approach.

"We have to remember that these are lifelong conditions," says Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism Skåne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people and their families.

"Because at a certain point in their adulthood during a clinical setting they have had their diagnosis removed, it doesn't necessarily mean that the ADHD or the autism has disappeared," he adds.

Symptoms could reappear later in life, he says. "The problem is once they resurface, that individual which doesn't have a diagnosis any longer, they will not be able to get the timely and correct support."

Lundström says he does not consider it a big risk that people could get reassessed and find themselves without necessary support.

During the pilot he encountered people who "really wanted" to get rid of their diagnoses but the psychologist said, "we still feel that you meet the criteria".

Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis which was initially given after she experienced a trauma.

"I didn't recognise myself in the description of autism," she says. "I was stuck. I know that this is not me, but I can't do anything about it."

It was requests from people like Johanna and Vilda that led to the establishment of the clinic, Lundström explains.

"It gained momentum by itself and the word spread around. A lot of people contacted us and we felt that there was a justification for starting up," he says. It is only open one day a month.

Before opening the clinic, Lundström conducted a small peer-reviewed study - of the 72 individuals who took part, roughly 80% did not meet the criteria for ADHD or autism. All the participants already wanted to lose their diagnosis, rather than being a randomly selected group.

"It's important to stress that this patient population is not necessarily representative for all with autism and ADHD," he adds.

During the first year of the pilot some 400 to 500 people spoke to Lundström, who is also associate professor of child and adolescent psychiatric sciences at the University of Gothenburg, about getting a reassessment.

The project also has the backing of senior figures in Swedish psychiatry, including Sophia Eberhard, a senior consultant specialising in child and adolescent psychiatry.

"It's psychiatry who in the beginning made those diagnoses," she says. "I believe we have a responsibility to help these young adults on their way."

In September, the BBC was given permission to join Freya as she became the first patient to attend the newly opened clinic, which serves both men and women.

During her appointment, Freya takes part in questionnaires and verbal assessments to see if she meets the ADHD criteria. The process is the same for both ADHD and autism, although the questions differ.

Freya says she is hopeful that she will be able to "get rid" of her ADHD diagnosis after the appointment.

But the doctors are adamant that they do not just give attendees the outcome they want. They conduct other checks such as assessing body language and communication skills, speaking to younger patients' parents, and checking medical files for ongoing treatment.

The opening of the clinic has drawn criticism from those who fear it sends the wrong message about autism and ADHD.

"The clinic presents neurodiversity and autistic people as a bad thing, like we are a problem that needs to be fixed - we are not," says Jenny Hedin, from charity Organiserade Autister Västernorrland, an advocacy organisation run by and for autistic adults.

Hedin, who is autistic and has ADHD, warns that people who can successfully "mask" or mimic neurotypical behaviour might feel under pressure to lose their diagnosis in order to be better accepted by society.

"That is especially a problem with women and girls, because girls are usually great at masking," she adds.

Others say the focus should be on changing the rules that make it difficult for people with ADHD or autism to pursue certain careers.

Eric Donell, the chairman of Riksförbundet Attention, a national Swedish charity, lobbies to remove employment restrictions affecting neurodivergent people, which he says are unfair.

He stresses that for many people, getting a diagnosis is extremely important. "Instead of asking people to get rid of their diagnosis, sometimes we should just ask whether the rules themselves are justified," he says.

Reassessments risk becoming "a way of adapting the individual to society instead of adapting society to human differences," he adds.

People from the UK, Denmark, Norway and Germany have also been in touch for reassessment, says Lundström, but they have been turned away, as the clinic only serves locals.

Georgina, 35, from the UK, contacted the clinic because she wants to have the autism diagnosis she received at 25 "removed".

"It felt like a magic spell, that I'd get this label and the world would be more understanding," she says.

Instead, she says, her colleagues belittled her.

Georgina has since been offered an NHS reassessment. The process is the same as the original assessment she went through, and can result in patients receiving more diagnoses, fewer diagnoses or no change.

The Swedish reassessment clinic says they generally would not apply new or additional diagnoses to people - something Georgina was attracted to.

"The situation where you can go in and then come out with other labels... that's really off-putting," she says. For now, she has decided not to undergo an NHS reassessment. Instead, she is trying to find out how often a diagnosis is reconsidered, before deciding whether to go ahead.

Back in Sweden, a few hours after Freya entered the clinic, she re-emerges from a consultation room. The doctors here have found that, right now, she does not meet the criteria for an ADHD diagnosis.

She says it is "confirmation" that she was right to question her diagnosis.

"Now, finally, I have the same opportunity as everyone else."

articles.title: At least 8 migrants dead, 6 airlifted to hospital after boat carrying 100 is rescued off Spain's Canary Islands
articles.summary: At least eight migrants have been found dead aboard a boat carrying around 100 people rescued off Spain's Canary Islands, maritime rescue authorities said
articles.body: At least eight migrants have been found dead aboard a boat carrying around 100 people rescued off Spain's Canary Islands, maritime rescue authorities said on Friday. Six others were seriously injured and airlifted to hospital.Between eight and 10 bodies were found aboard the boat, maritime rescuers told AFP. The vessel was discovered 39 nautical miles (72 km) south of El Hierro and was being towed towards the port of La Estaca, according to rescue authorities.Six seriously injured migrants were evacuated by helicopter to El Hierro, while 84 others, including a child, were brought ashore at La Restinga. One person chose to remain on the boat, the sea rescue service said.An AFP journalist at the port reported seeing migrants being assisted by Civil Guard officers, Red Cross workers and soldiers from the army's emergency response unit. Some survivors were carried ashore on stretchers, while others were wrapped in thermal blankets.The tragedy comes as immigration has emerged as a major issue in Spain's general election campaign. Right-wing opposition parties have accused prime minister Pedro Sanchez's government of failing to control the country's borders and criticised its more open migration policy.Alberto Nunez Feijoo, leader of the main opposition Popular Party (PP), said on X, "People losing their lives at sea is the worst consequence of this government's irresponsibility.""Spain urgently needs an orderly migration policy that can prevent tragedies like this one," he added.Far-right Vox party leader Santiago Abascal also criticised the government, denouncing what he described as the "abandonment of parts" of Spain, including Ceuta and El Hierro.Most opinion polls suggest the PP could win the most seats but fall short of an overall majority, potentially requiring support from Vox to form a government.Canary Islands face mounting pressureAccording to Spanish interior ministry figures, 24,364 migrants reached the Canary Islands between January 1 and November 15, compared with 14,690 during the same period in 2025. More than 11,000 arrivals were recorded in the first half of November alone.The archipelago recorded an unprecedented 2,100 arrivals in a single day on November 25, most of them on El Hierro, which has a population of around 11,400, according to news agency Reuters.Regional leader Fernando Clavijo called for urgent intervention from Madrid and the European Commission, including the deployment of Frontex, the European Union's border agency."A lot of pain and feeling of impotence over this new tragedy," Clavijo said on X."The humanitarian emergency doesn't start on El Hierro, but on the shores of Senegal and Gambia, where we have to act," he added.Sanchez said on public television on Wednesday that his government had been working with Senegalese and Gambian authorities on border controls to reduce departures.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Montana widow's estate was denied a share of her late husband's property after officials used tax assessments to value land in two states; the Supreme Court has ordered a new look at the inheritance
articles.summary: Montana’s Supreme Court has ordered a lower court to reconsider whether the estate of a deceased Montana woman is entitled to a share of her late
articles.body: Montana’s Supreme Court has ordered a lower court to reconsider whether the estate of a deceased Montana woman is entitled to a share of her late husband’s property. The case involves Jack Raymond Stone, who died in 2017, and his wife, Sara Benchoff Stone, who sought a spousal elective share after learning that most of Jack’s assets had passed outside probate. Sara died shortly afterward, and her son, Ed, continued the claim as executor of her estate, as per the court report on Justia U.S. Law.The dispute turned on how officials valued land in Montana and Texas. The estate’s special administrator used tax assessment values rather than independent appraisals, concluded that no elective share was owed, and the Fergus County District Court approved that approach. On November 24, the Montana Supreme Court reversed key parts of that ruling and sent the case back for a new valuation process. Read more details about this case, as per the report, here:What the family disputedJack and Sara had been married for just under 23 years when Jack died at age 86. Although Jack left no will, he had arranged for nearly all of his assets to pass outside probate through beneficiary designations to Sara and his children from a prior marriage, Robin McCroskey and Bryant Stone. Sara filed for probate and sought an elective share, a legal mechanism that can give a surviving spouse a portion of a deceased spouse’s augmented estate even when most assets bypass probate.Sara died in June 2018, less than a year after Jack. Her son Ed became executor of her estate and replaced her as the person pursuing the claim. The special administrator, Stacie Arntzen, valued Jack’s assets at about $2.89 million and calculated that transfers to Sara totaled $529,625.79, while transfers to Robin and Bryant totaled $1.13 million and $1.21 million respectively.After those transfers, only $21,854.61 remained in the probate estate. That money was quickly depleted defending a malpractice lawsuit against Jack’s estate, which settled for $69,000. Sara’s estate contributed $34,500 to the settlement, while Robin and Bryant each contributed $17,250 from funds they had received outside probate.The valuation problemThe central issue was whether tax assessment figures could be treated as reliable measures of fair market value for the elective-share calculation. The special administrator used cadastral tax values for surface real estate in both Montana and Texas and concluded that Sara’s estate was not entitled to an elective share. Ed objected, particularly to the valuation of Jack’s Montana agricultural property.The district court accepted the approach and barred Ed from introducing appraisal evidence concerning Jack’s Montana land. It relied on judicial estoppel, a doctrine that can prevent a party from taking contradictory positions in court. The court reasoned that Ed had used tax values in an inventory for Sara’s Texas estate, so he should also be bound to tax values for Jack’s Montana property.The Montana Supreme Court rejected that reasoning. It said the Texas inventory did not establish that Ed had taken an inconsistent position about the value of Jack’s Montana property. Ed had expressly accepted the Texas values for Sara’s estate but wanted to present evidence about the value of a different property in a different state.Why tax values matteredThe court explained that Montana law generally requires taxable property to be appraised at 100 percent of market value, but agricultural land is treated differently. State law directs the Department of Revenue to value bona fide agricultural property based on its agricultural use, excluding value attributable to urban influences or speculative purposes.That distinction matters because a property’s agricultural-use assessment may be legally valid for tax purposes while still understating what a buyer would pay on the open market. The Supreme Court said that using the same label, “tax value,” for properties in Montana and Texas did not prove that the figures were equivalent or that they represented fair market value.The special administrator argued that appraisals would add expense and delay to an already lengthy estate case, especially because the estate had little cash. The Supreme Court acknowledged that courts may consider cost, delay, and liquidity when managing probate proceedings. But it said those concerns did not justify treating disputed tax values as conclusive when a party offered to pay for an appraisal.The court’s rulingJustice Ingrid Gustafson wrote the unanimous opinion reversing the district court’s rulings on judicial estoppel, the use of tax values, and the denial of Ed’s offer of proof. The court said the trial judge abused discretion by making the tax figures conclusive despite Ed’s objection and by preventing him from preserving appraisal evidence for appeal.The Supreme Court did not decide that Jack’s Montana property is worth more than the tax assessment suggested. It also did not decide that Sara’s estate will receive an elective share. Instead, it ordered the district court to allow relevant valuation evidence, determine the fair market value of Jack’s Montana property as of his death on August 13, 2017, and recalculate any elective share that may be due.The court made clear that tax values are not automatically excluded. It said the trial court may consider reliable tax-value evidence, but it must also give the parties a reasonable opportunity to present competing valuation evidence and decide the issue on a record sufficient for review.What it means for estatesThe decision is important for families dealing with farmland, ranchland, mineral interests, and other property whose tax assessment may differ from its market value. A tax assessment is designed primarily for taxation, while fair market value asks what a willing buyer would pay a willing seller under normal conditions. Those figures can be close in some cases, but they can diverge sharply for agricultural land affected by development pressure, water rights, mineral value, or speculative demand.For executors and estate administrators, the ruling reinforces that efficiency cannot replace accuracy when a valuation directly affects a beneficiary’s inheritance. The court said the duty to administer an estate efficiently does not displace the legal requirement to determine fair market value. It also noted that a qualified and disinterested appraiser may assist with valuation, although a certified appraisal is not required for every asset.For now, the estate remains unresolved. The Montana Supreme Court’s remand gives Ed’s side another opportunity to show what Jack’s Montana land was actually worth when he died, and whether that value changes the amount owed to Sara’s estate.You use AI every day. articles.title: US battered by Thanksgiving storms: Hundreds of thousands without power as floods wreak havoc
articles.summary: Hundreds of thousands of homes and businesses across the United States remained without electricity, a day after powerful Thanksgiving storms battered the
articles.body: Hundreds of thousands of homes and businesses across the United States remained without electricity, a day after powerful Thanksgiving storms battered the East Coast, triggering floods, damaging buildings and disrupting transport. Power restoration was under way, even as coastal flood warnings and strong winds continued across parts of the region.More than 500,000 customers remained without electricity on Friday, down from a peak of over 900,000 on Thursday, according to outage tracking website PowerOutage.us. Pennsylvania and New Jersey accounted for the largest number of affected customers.The National Weather Service said conditions across the eastern US were expected to improve, but warned that the system would take time to weaken. "But this huge system will take some time to weaken," it said on its website.Blustery winds of 25 to 35 mph (40 to 56 kph), with stronger gusts, were forecast across the East. Coastal flood warnings remained in force from New Jersey to Virginia through Friday.Flooding, rescues and damage reported across statesThe storms disrupted holiday travel, brought down trees and power lines, and prompted water rescues across several states. In Norfolk, Virginia, emergency crews rescued 39 people and two dogs, City Councilman Tommy Smigiel said in a post.In Virginia Beach, part of a fishing pier collapsed, prompting authorities to close a three-mile stretch of beach, including the boardwalk, "due to dangerous conditions", the city said.Building roofs also collapsed in Ocean City and Rockville. In Avalon, New Jersey, businesses were pumping out seawater after unusually high tides flooded parts of the seaside community."Conditions were a million times better than they were 24 hours ago," borough business administrator Scott Wahl told news agency AP.Meanwhile, nearly two million water customers in Maryland's Montgomery and Prince George's counties were allowed to resume normal consumption on Friday after being asked to conserve supplies during the storm.Snow, coastal flooding add to weather disruptionsThe storm system also brought snowfall across parts of the Midwest and southern US. Eastern Missouri recorded up to 15 inches (38 cm) of snow on Thursday, the National Weather Service said. Parts of Tennessee remained under a winter storm warning, with snowfall of up to an inch forecast.On the Pacific coast, high tides triggered flooding and disrupted rail services. Amtrak's Pacific Surfliner cancelled or shortened more than a dozen services between San Diego and Los Angeles, deploying buses for affected passengers.In Hampton, Virginia, strong winds toppled the much-visited "Grieving Tree", also known as the "Shell Tree", at Grandview Beach.Further damage was reported in Delaware, where resident Cynthia Battles, 70, said waves had crashed through her waterfront cottage, destroying boats and damaging belongings.You use AI every day. articles.title: Eetha, Maharashtra's Vithabhai Narayangaonkar: The 'Tamasha queen' of India whose fans paid for a show that never happened
articles.summary: A new Bollywood flim spotlights the remarkable life of dancer and singer Vithabhai Narayangaonkar.
articles.body:
Few things could keep Vithabai Narayangaonkar, one of the greatest stars of Maharashtra's folk theatre, away from the stage.

Not even, it would seem, the birth of her child.

In the 1960s, the singer, dancer and troupe leader was performing in Shikhar Shingnapur, a village in the western Indian state, when she went into labour.

"She quietly stepped behind the stage into a makeshift tent while the rest of us continued performing," her daughter, veteran folk artist Mangala Bansode, told BBC Marathi.

Outside, the restless audience kept shouting: "Where is Vitha?"

When Vithabai returned to the stage, she was cradling her newborn son, the seventh of her eight children.

"The audience was stunned, but they quietly left, saying, 'We will watch your performance later'," Bansode recalled.

Outspoken and quick-witted, Vithabai held audiences across Maharashtra in thrall for decades, earning the title of Tamasha Samradnyi – the empress of Tamasha, the state's traditional travelling folk theatre.

Now, more than two decades after her death, her life has inspired a Bollywood musical, Eetha, starring Shraddha Kapoor, and due for release on 4 December.

Directed by Laxman Utekar, Eetha is based on Yogiraj Bagul's Marathi book chronicling Vithabai's life.

Rooted in devotional poetry, Tamasha evolved into a lively mix of music, dance, comedy and drama. At its heart is Lavani, a song and dance tradition in which verses ranging from the bawdy to the politically incisive are performed to the beat of the dholki, a percussion instrument.

Eetha evokes the world of Tamasha in its heyday. Kapoor, who had never performed Lavani before, learnt to dance while wearing musical anklets weighing 4kg each.

"The lives of Tamasha artists have been very tough, so in their dance you see pain as well as joy," Kapoor recalled at a promotional event.

Many Tamasha performers, including Vithabai, came from oppressed castes, facing discrimination even as their artistry drew large crowds.

How much of that history Eetha will capture remains debated. Utekar says it is not a biopic, but his decision to rename the protagonist Vithabai Bhau Gavkar instead of Vithabai Bhau Mang Narayangaonkar has drawn criticism.

For critics, much of Vithabai's history was contained in her name – Mang identified her with a historically oppressed Dalit community, while Narayangaonkar spoke of her family's roots in Narayangaon village. Both featured in the name of the troupe she inherited from her father – Bhau-Bapu Mang Narayangaonkar Tamasha Mandal.

Vithabai spoke openly about caste and the indignities Tamasha artists faced, themes that also surfaced in her songs. In a 1960s Lavani documented by historian Shailaja Paik, she rebuked men for lewd gestures, reminding them she danced to earn a living, not to please them.

It was a livelihood she had inherited from generations of performers in her family.

Like her son, Vithabai was born during a Tamasha performance, in 1935. Her mother, Shanta, had continued touring with her husband Bhau's troupe throughout her pregnancy.

Vithabai joined a theatre group at eight and her father's troupe at 13, soon becoming its star. After her father and co-leader Bapu died in quick succession, she took over the troupe with her husband and cousin.

Her career flourished during Tamasha's golden age, when productions grew more elaborate, drawing on mythology, history and contemporary life, says folk arts scholar Sukhada Khandge.

Khandge, who watched Vithabai perform as a child, recalls her sparkling eyes and commanding presence. She was as expressive with her face as she was with her feet.

Her fame carried her beyond Maharashtra.

During India's war with China in 1962, Vithabai performed for soldiers in the North-East Frontier Agency, now largely Arunachal Pradesh, braving freezing conditions just three months after giving birth, Bansode says.

At a conference in 1996, she recalled meeting soldiers from the historically oppressed Mahar and Mang communities at the frontier.

"Our Mahar-Mang soldiers were expected to fight and lay down their lives defending the nation, but the very same people would not even allow our bridegroom to pass through the village entrance," she said.

Despite offers from leading filmmakers, including Raj Kapoor, and roles in Marathi cinema, Vithabai refused to leave theatre. Film fame, she felt, would benefit her alone, while her troupe supported some 50 families, Bansode says.

There was a tenderness, too, in her relationship with audiences.

In his book on Vithabai's life, which inspired Eetha, Yogiraj Bagul recounts a performance in Mumbai during Diwali in 1971.

Despite the threat of rain, spectators insisted on buying tickets, saying the money would be their Bhau Beej gift to Vithabai if the show was cancelled – a festival celebrating the bond between brothers and sisters.

When the rain came, people left chanting: "Bhau Beej, Bhau Beej."

But Vithabai's fortunes failed to match her fame. Her husband, Maruti Sawant, mismanaged the troupe's finances and took loans in her name, family members say. By the time she left him in 1982, she was heavily indebted.

Bagul also writes about a 1986 column in a Marathi daily that revealed how the empress of Tamasha was now travelling on public buses and staying in cheap accommodation.

Despite public support, Vithabai was forced to disband her troupe in 1990 – the same year she received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award, one of India's highest performing arts honours.

Vithabai successfully campaigned for government pensions for Tamasha artists. But many of the hardships she knew persist today, says Marathi writer Pradnya Daya Pawar.

Troupes spend nearly eight months a year on the road, with performers struggling to feed their children and educate them, she says. Despite government aid, many remain indebted to private moneylenders.

Vithabai's financial struggles persisted until her death in January 2002. Her family could pay only 4,000 of the 5,900 rupees owed to the Pune hospital where she died, the Times of India reported.

Fellow artists and admirers chipped in to bring her body home to Narayangaon.

Maharashtra has since instituted a lifetime achievement award in her name.

Eetha could now introduce Vithabai to a generation that never saw her perform, though the changes to her name have left some uneasy.

Marathi writer Pragya Daya Pawar argues that omitting the reference to Vithabai's caste risks obscuring the difficulties she confronted.

"It erases the social location, struggle and resistance that shaped her remarkable journey, reducing an extraordinary artist's story to a purely individual achievement," she says.

But Bansode, who spent years performing alongside her mother, says there is much to celebrate.

"The name doesn't matter to me. I am simply proud that a film is being made about my mother," she says.

articles.title: Taiwan votes in high-stakes local elections as China watches closely
articles.summary: Voters in Taiwan went to the polls on Saturday to elect mayors, county chiefs, council members and other local representatives across 22 cities and
articles.body: Voters in Taiwan went to the polls on Saturday to elect mayors, county chiefs, council members and other local representatives across 22 cities and counties. The closely watched contest could indicate party support ahead of the island’s 2028 presidential election, with China monitoring the outcome.Polling stations opened at 8 am local time and were scheduled to close at 4 pm (local time), with results expected later in the day. The winners will serve four-year terms. The Associated Press (AP) reported that campaigning largely centred on local issues, including transport and the environment, although tensions with Beijing remained an important backdrop.The main contest is between the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and the opposition Kuomintang (KMT), which has traditionally performed strongly in local elections. In the 2022 vote, the KMT won 14 cities and counties, while the DPP secured five. The remaining three went to other parties or independent candidates, Reuters reported.President Lai Ching-te campaigned for DPP candidates, appearing at a rally in Taoyuan City on Thursday to support his party’s mayoral nominee. The DPP is seeking to improve its local standing as political parties begin positioning themselves for the next presidential and parliamentary elections in early 2028.Taipei’s mayoral contest has emerged as one of the most closely watched races. Incumbent Mayor Chiang Wan-an, of the KMT, is facing a strong challenge from DPP candidate Puma Shen, an academic-turned-lawmaker known for his work on China’s information operations.China has denounced Shen and says he is wanted by Chinese police for “separatism”. Shen told Reuters this month that Chinese police had never contacted him. He also said the result would represent a victory for democracy in the face of pressure from Beijing, regardless of who won.Beijing claims Taiwan as its territory and has increased pressure on the self-governed island to accept its sovereignty claims, which Taipei rejects. Taiwan’s government also warned voters ahead of the election to remain alert to false claims on social media, citing what it described as continuing Chinese disinformation efforts.The security backdrop intensified on Friday after Taiwan’s Defence Ministry said it had detected 30 Chinese military aircraft operating around the island. It said 26 crossed the Taiwan Strait’s median line during a “joint combat readiness patrol” involving warships.Other key mayoral contests are being held in New Taipei City, the island’s most populous city, and Kaohsiung, a traditional DPP stronghold. articles.title: UK flu vaccine: Who should get it this winter and why?
articles.summary: Amid a surge in influenza, health officials are urging people to get a vaccine - but what if you're young and healthy?
articles.body:
Health officials are urging more people to take up the offer of a free flu vaccine as the number of hospital patients seriously ill with the virus has risen sharply in the past week.

The flu surge has come slightly early this year but that is not completely unusual.

Flu activity is still at "moderate levels" and the peak may not arrive until December or early January, health officials warn.

So what is the advice on getting a vaccine, who can get it for free and who should pay?

"If you're offered it, it's a good idea to have it," says Prof Nick Hopkinson, professor of respiratory medicine at Imperial College London.

"The main reason is to avoid serious complications in vulnerable groups – so as many as possible should have it in those groups.

"People don't understand it's a potentially life-threatening infection and that the vaccine is safe."

Flu is a viral infection which affects the nose, throat and lungs. Often it goes away on its own but it can make people seriously ill – complications can include pneumonia, heart attacks and other underlying illnesses getting worse.

In England last winter, UKHSA estimated there were 3,798 deaths attributed to influenza.

Scientists have to predict which strains of influenza will be circulating before the vaccine is manufactured each year in time for winter.

The current one protects against three strains – two influenza A strains and one influenza B strain.

Even if these strains drift slightly, experts say getting vaccinated is still a good idea to lower the risk of severe illness.

Millions of vulnerable people are eligible for the free jab to help protect them against flu, including children, pregnant women, care home residents, people with lung conditions and anyone aged 65 and over.

But only around a third of under-65s and two-thirds of those aged 65 and over have been vaccinated so far this winter.

That leaves around seven million people unprotected at present, health officials say.

Parents are being urged to vaccinate young children in order to protect them and other people they come into contact with.

Can I still get flu if I've been vaccinated?

Yes. The vaccine does not rule out the possibility you will get flu, but it does reduce the chances you'll become very ill with it and end up in hospital.

It takes two weeks for your body's immunity to build up after being vaccinated, which is another reason to have the jab sooner rather than later.

Protection from the vaccine reduces the risk of serious flu complications by 50%, says Prof Hopkinson.

If you are not eligible for the free flu vaccine, you can still buy it from most pharmacies for between £15 and 25.

"It's a reasonable thing to consider," says Prof Hopkinson.

But it is far more important for the millions of vulnerable people offered it free to be vaccinated.

They are known to be at risk of health complications from the virus.

Other groups are also at risk: "Smokers are five times more likely to get flu – so quit now," he suggests.

Am I depriving someone else if I buy the jab?

There are different vaccines for those getting it free on the NHS and those paying for it privately.

However, the vaccines do the same job and protect against the same strains of flu.

Pharmacist Olivier Picard says he's seen a "massive spike in demand" for flu jabs in the last 24 hours.

More people are booking an appointment for a free vaccine they have already been reminded about, and others are asking about paying for it themselves.

"When it gets cold, people tend to wake up to getting the free jab and want it before Christmas," he says.

He says there is no issue with supplies of the vaccine at present and "plenty in the system".

articles.title: Poundland: 'I don't know what I'd do without it,' say shoppers as chain fights for survival
articles.summary: The discount retailer has collapsed into administration after its US owners failed to secure a rescue deal.
articles.body:
For Charlie Franklyn, a trip to Poundland is almost as routine as going to work.

The care worker from Teesside pops into her local branch nearly every day – it's where she buys cleaning products, beauty bargains and the budget-friendly finds she loves sharing online.

Charlie has been creating social media content for five years, and Poundland is one of her regular filming spots.

Her videos showcasing the store and its wares have proved popular, and although she's never been paid by the retailer, she's been gifted products over the years and built relationships with staff who invite her in to film.

"For me, Poundland is more than just a shopping stop. I buy so many things from there that are much cheaper than in other shops."

'We don't need empty shops on the high street'

The budget retailer has gone into administration, putting 11,000 jobs at risk in the run-up to Christmas. For now, its 600 stores continue to trade as usual but they will eventually close if a buyer can't be found to rescue some or all of the business.

Charlie says she was "surprised by the news" and is worried about what it could mean for shoppers like her.

"With the cost-of-living crisis going on, places like Poundland are so important and we really don't need empty shops on the high street," she tells the BBC.

Other shoppers the BBC spoke to are equally concerned. Kimi Browne, 26, from London, doesn't often shop at Poundland but relies on it for seasonal bargains, including Halloween decorations and accessories for her clothes.

She says the retailer is "an important part of the community as it offers affordable products for families".

Rea Catedrilla has a friend who works at the Poundland store in Notting Hill and feels "sad and sorry" for those who could lose their jobs.

She visits Poundland around four times per week because "it's less expensive than other shops and it's very convenient".

Poundland opened its first store in Burton-upon-Trent in 1990 and grew into one of the UK's best-known discount retailers, with 900 shops across the country at its peak.

But rising costs and competition from supermarkets such as Aldi and Lidl put pressure on the business and, in June 2025, it was sold to US investment firm Gordon Brothers for a nominal £1.

There had been signs of a recovery – Poundland made a profit of £18.1m in the year to September, compared with a £68m loss the previous year. But Gordon Brothers insists the business has missed its budget forecasts and would continue to struggle even if only its worst-performing stores were closed.

News of the administration has left many Poundland staff on edge. Aboud, 39, who manages the Camden branch in north London, says it feels like a "slap in the face", as he thought the chain had started to recover over the last 18 months.

"Everything we've worked hard for was for nothing. Someone has come in and dismantled all that effort."

Aboud says his colleagues at the store have been emotional and that it's "very worrying to have a job at risk given the current climate".

But he adds that his team "are still hopeful" that a buyer could rescue the chain and that they continue to give "100% regardless of the circumstances".

Retail expert Mary Portas said that when Poundland first opened, it was "everything under one roof that you didn't even know you wanted or needed" but it failed to keep pace as the market evolved.

While inflation has made it harder to sustain the £1 pricing model, other discount retailers have also made value shopping a more appealing experience, she says.

"Value brands, instead of looking shabby, which quite frankly Poundland often did, have taken themselves into a much better place," she says.

"On so many levels, Poundland just felt like yesterday's business."

The company has now appointed consultancy AlixPartners to oversee a sale of part or all of the discount retailer. Administrators will decide whether to sell the business as a whole or break it up, with the latter considered the more likely outcome.

Helen Howes, Poundland's store manager in Camborne, Cornwall, says she wishes staff "could have been told more at times".

She adds that losing Poundland would be "devastating" for the town as it's one of its larger shops and an important draw for shoppers.

Jilly, who shops at the branch in Ealing, says the store has been a "godsend" and that it would be a blow to the local community if it closed.

Her shopping trolley is filled with everything from cleaning products and stationery to "upmarket things that I will gift for Christmas".

"It's tragic, everyone losing their jobs just before Christmas," she adds.
