articles.title: Two American Airlines planes clip wings while taxiing at Washington airport; FAA to probe
articles.summary: Two American Airlines planes clipped each other's wings on Friday while taxiing for departure at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Washington
articles.body: Two American Airlines planes clipped each other's wings on Friday while taxiing for departure at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Washington DC, United States, prompting an emergency response.As per the BBC, no injuries were reported, and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said it would investigate the incident."American Airlines Flight 638 clipped the wing of American Airlines Flight 2152 while taxiing for departure," the FAA said in a statement. The incident occurred at around 5.10pm ET (22:10 GMT).Flight 2152 was bound for Chicago's O'Hare International Airport, while Flight 638 was scheduled to fly to Dallas-Fort Worth, BBC reported.Both aircraft returned to their gates and were taken out of service for inspection by maintenance teams, American Airlines said. The airline added that the wingtips of both Boeing 737-800 aircraft had made contact. It is working to arrange onward travel for passengers evacuated from the two planes.Air traffic controllers can be heard in an audio recording saying that two Boeing 737s had clipped wings on the airport's runway. They requested an emergency response and fire personnel at the aircraft before directing both planes to return to their gates.A passenger on Flight 2152 told the BBC that he felt a "large jolt" on the right side of the aircraft as it was taxiing before departure. He said the "aircraft shook quite violently" upon impact and passengers inside the cabin gasped. He described the moment as "tense", but said nobody appeared to be injured.Looking out of the window, the passenger saw a piece of the aircraft lying on the ground, which he said appeared to be the "tip of the wing". He also noticed that the other aircraft's wing was overlapping the wing of his plane. As the aircraft taxied back to the gate, he saw a truck collecting the fallen piece.The passenger said the fact that this was not the first incident at the airport was "definitely scary".The incident took place at the same airport where 67 people were killed in January 2025 when a passenger jet collided with an Army helicopter.You use AI every day. articles.title: Spa, jacuzzi: Delhi govt displays 'Sheesh Mahal'
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi govt Friday opened former chief minister Arvind Kejriwal's 6 Flagstaff Road residence, dubbed 'Sheesh Mahal' by BJP, for a media tour.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi govt Friday opened former chief minister Arvind Kejriwal's 6 Flagstaff Road residence, dubbed 'Sheesh Mahal' by BJP, for a media tour.Large boards reading "Welcome to Sheesh Mahal, built at a cost of Rs 58 crore" greeted visitors at the entrance. BJP also arranged for a Kejriwal lookalike to welcome mediapersons and show them around the bungalow.From curtains and chandeliers to television sets and sofas, household items had their "price tags" on display. While the fittings in a powder room were valued at Rs 5.8 lakh, a 'baithak' cost Rs 41 lakh and a lobby had items "worth around Rs 7.5 lakh". Among the other items on display were a "Rs 30 lakh" TV unit, a "Rs 11.6 lakh" chandelier and a "Rs 5.5 lakh" two-seater sofa.The lifts, refrigerator and dining table had their “prices” displayed too.The bungalow, maintained by Public Works Department (PWD), has eight bedrooms, 13 toilets, a jacuzzi bath, a spa and five OLED TVs, among other amenities.The bungalow will be opened to the public next month, with an online ticket-booking system likely to be put in place. According to officials, the entry fee is likely to be around Rs 20, while senior citizens and college students will be allowed free entry. From Monday, BJP is likely to organise guided tours for different sections of society, including lawyers, intellectuals and senior citizens.Chief minister Rekha Gupta said the people of Delhi had long wanted to see the bungalow and that residents of Punjab should also get an opportunity to visit it. “This was very important. The people of Delhi wanted to see this Sheesh Mahal, and we want the people of Punjab to see it too. First, they looted Delhi, and now they are looting Punjab,” she alleged.Claiming that the tour had once again exposed AAP before the public, Gupta urged people to visit the bungalow.AAP did not respond to the allegations. The party had earlier accused BJP of inflating the expenditure figures and maintained that the bungalow was developed as the official residence of the chief minister, not for Kejriwal personally, and that any future CM would be entitled to live there.PWD minister Parvesh Verma said, “We are just showing how Arvind Kejriwal spent the public money. He used to say that he won’t use govt vehicle or govt residence, but went on to spend Rs 56 crore on this govt bungalow.”Former AAP member Prashant Bhushan also took a swipe at Kejriwal. “Aam Aadmi Party chief Kejriwal’s Sheesh Mahal is now open to public. Built with expensive jacuzzi, sauna, massage table, barber’s chair and 10 TVs of Rs 10 lakh each, this residence of the Aam Aadmi cost the exchequer only Rs 58 crore,” he said.Kejriwal’s former official residence has been at the centre of a long-running political controversy over allegations of extravagant expenditure on its renovation. BJP had alleged that Rs 45-52 crore of public money was spent on the interiors alone. Allegations of financial irregularities and violations of building norms also led to multiple inquiries, including those initiated by the lieutenant governor, Central Vigilance Commission and CBI.According to a Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) report tabled in Delhi Assembly, the renovation of Kejriwal’s then official residence was completed at a cost of Rs 33.7 crore, 342% above the estimated cost. Of this, Rs 18.9 crore was spent on “superior specifications, artistic, antique and ornamental” items.Kejriwal lived in the bungalow with his family from 2015 until Oct 2024, when he vacated it after stepping down as CM.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Taliban reportedly strips women of their names in Afghan province, now being called 'goat' or 'grandmother'
articles.summary: The Taliban reportedly banned women's names from official records in an Afghan province, five years after reclaiming power amid Biden's chaotic withdrawal.
articles.body: The Taliban have reportedly banned the use of women's names in official documents in a northern Afghan province, with some women being referred to by degrading animal names, according to a report by Spanish newspaper El País. The latest assault on women's rights under Taliban rule reportedly extends to medical records and prescriptions in Afghanistan's Balkh province, raising fears that the restrictions could spread nationwide. Healthcare workers and other public employees have been instructed to address women as "Bibi," meaning grandmother or old woman, according to reporting by Afghan news outlet Zan Times and The Guardian cited by El País. MOSCOW, TALIBAN FORGE MILITARY ALLIANCE IN POWER GRAB AFTER US AFGHANISTAN EXIT: REPORTS Afghan women's rights activist Lalah Osmany, who is based in Germany, told El País that testimony from women, doctors and civil rights activists indicates some women are also being referred to in degrading terms such as "goat" or "cow." "This is a systematic process of dehumanization," Osmany told the newspaper. An Afghan activist speaking under a pseudonym confirmed the reported order to El País, although she said it had so far been ignored. Zubaida Akbar, who directs the Afghanistan program at women's rights organization Femena, warned that the Taliban could eventually impose the ban nationwide, citing previous instances in which local restrictions were expanded across the country. IRAN FLOGS FEMALE SINGER 74 TIMES FOR PERFORMING WITHOUT HIJAB IN VIRAL YOUTUBE CONCERT Femena has counted more than 144 decrees restricting Afghan women's rights, according to El País. Girls have been barred from studying beyond age 12, while women have been shut out of most professions and subjected to restrictions on speaking in public, the newspaper reported.Some Afghan women have resorted to running underground businesses and secret schools in defiance of Taliban restrictions, according to Associated Press reporting published Nov. 17. IRAN TO EXECUTE FIRST FEMALE PROTESTER TIED TO ANTI-REGIME UNREST One Kabul beauty salon owner, whose identity was concealed for her safety, reopened her business after authorities raided her previous salon and confiscated her equipment. "But now, they won’t even allow that; for women in Afghanistan, working has become a crime," she told the AP. An assistant teacher at a secret school in Kabul described living in constant fear of arrest. "We are absolutely terrified of that possibility," she told the AP. Mohammad Aslam, a spokesman for the Taliban's Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice, defended the broader restrictions in comments to the AP, saying women could conduct business and social affairs provided they adhered to Islamic Sharia law and existing laws. Osmany also warned that the reported naming ban could endanger female patients by increasing the risk of medical errors if prescriptions and medical records are filed under identical names. Afghan women already face severe barriers to medical care under Taliban rule, including restrictions on male doctors treating female patients and bans on women pursuing medical training, according to El País. In 2017, Osmany launched a campaign to have Afghan women's names included on official documents, including their children's birth certificates. ARMY VET LAWMAKER MARKS ABBEY GATE ANNIVERSARY WITH BLISTERING MESSAGE FOR BIDEN-HARRIS: 'ABJECT FAILURE' Despite receiving death threats from extremists, her campaign helped secure a change in 2020 allowing mothers' names to be voluntarily included on such documents. That progress was short-lived. The Taliban swept back into power in August 2021 as the U.S.-backed Afghan government collapsed amid then-President Joe Biden's chaotic military withdrawal, leaving the country once again under the control of Islamist extremists. The withdrawal drew widespread condemnation after 13 American service members, mostly Marines, were killed in an ISIS-K terrorist attack during the evacuation from Kabul. Biden faced further backlash from Gold Star families after checking his watch during the dignified transfer of fallen American troops at Dover Air Force Base in Delaware. Five years later, Afghan women and girls have seen hard-won freedoms stripped away under Taliban rule. Now, activists warn, even their very identities are under threat. articles.summary: NAVI MUMBAI: A 45-day search operation by the Khopoli police, launched on Oct 7, 2026, ended with the rescue of 23-year-old techie Rahul Mishra from
articles.body: NAVI MUMBAI: A 45-day search operation by the Khopoli police, launched on Oct 7, 2026, ended with the rescue of 23-year-old techie Rahul Mishra from Nagpur, who was traced to Ramdevra in Rajasthan's Jaisalmer district, where he was working at a hotel. The police suspect that Mishra had orchestrated his disappearance, staging a possible accident, murder and kidnapping drama to evade action by the cybercrime police following a complaint lodged by his girlfriend's family.According to the Khopoli police, intimate moments between Mishra and his girlfriend, a resident of Adilabad in Telangana, had allegedly surfaced on pornographic websites. Following this, her family approached the local cybercrime cell. Mishra had reportedly fallen in love with the woman while working with her on an information technology project.Mishra allegedly abandoned his motorcycle, left an empty bag and footwear by the roadside, and placed an iPhone nearby. The phone was later found to be fake. His helmet was discovered in a valley about 10 feet below road level. Joggers who suspected an accident or suicide alerted the Khopoli police, following which a kidnapping case was registered.Police investigated the matter from multiple angles, including accident, murder - as alleged by Mishra's family-and kidnapping.The extensive search operation included four days of combing the Garmal Ghat section along the Mumbai-Pune Expressway link, with drones and four rescue teams deployed. Rescuers also descended 500-600 feet into the valley but found no trace of Mishra.The case drew considerable attention, with the Khopoli police receiving frequent calls from the offices of the chief minister, Union minister Nitin Gadkari, and state revenue minister Chandrashekhar Bawankule. Khopoli Police Inspector Sachin Hire said, "Our technical investigation and questioning of around 110 people eventually helped us trace him to Rajasthan. Mishra returned to Akola on Nov 23 and subsequently his home in Nagpur."Stay updated with the latest Navi Mumbai news. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: A grandmother in Arizona sent a Thanksgiving invitation to the wrong number in 2016; ten years later, she and the stranger who joined her family dinner are working with writers on a movie about their friendship
articles.summary: A wrong-number text message changed the lives of Arizona grandmother Wanda Dench and Jamal Hinton, who was 17 when he received her Thanksgiving invitation
articles.body: A wrong-number text message changed the lives of Arizona grandmother Wanda Dench and Jamal Hinton, who was 17 when he received her Thanksgiving invitation in 2016. What began as an unexpected dinner invitation developed into a friendship that has continued for a decade. Now, the two are taking their story to the screen through a film being developed with Lifetime.The project is expected to be released around Thanksgiving next year, CNN reported. Dench and Hinton are working with the channel's writers while also preparing for another family gathering this holiday season. They recently met on a park bench in Arizona to discuss their plans, which include coordinating celebrations with their growing families and attending media interviews.Their friendship attracted widespread attention after Hinton shared the unusual exchange that brought them together. Dench had meant to invite one of her grandchildren to Thanksgiving dinner but accidentally sent the message to Hinton's number. He responded with a selfie, making it clear that she had contacted the wrong person. He also asked whether the invitation still included a plate of food.Dench welcomed him anyway. Hinton accepted and turned up at her Phoenix-area home, where she and her husband, Lonnie, received him as a guest. That decision became the beginning of a tradition that has continued through several major changes in both their lives.A friendship that continued beyond the viral momentThe story received attention in 2016, when the US was dealing with racial tensions, political divisions and the aftermath of the deadly shooting at the Pulse nightclub in Florida. The unexpected friendship between a grandmother and a teenager from different backgrounds became a widely shared positive story.Dench initially thought the attention would fade after a short period. However, the public continued following their relationship, particularly through their annual Thanksgiving celebrations."The first year when it all happened, I thought we'll have that 15 minutes of fame, like everybody gets, and then everybody will forget about it," Dench told CNN. "It really surprises both of us that every year the media comes back."The gatherings have not been identical every year. Family circumstances have changed, some relatives are no longer present, and new people have become part of the celebrations. Yet Dench and Hinton have maintained their connection and have marked almost every Thanksgiving together.Their relationship has also continued outside the holiday tradition. They have supported each other through personal milestones and difficult periods. Lonnie died in 2020 due to complications from Covid-19. Dench was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2024 and has since become cancer-free. Hinton has also entered a new phase of life after getting married recently.The attention surrounding their story has brought interviews and sponsorship offers from major brands. However, neither wants their public image to define their entire life.Hinton wants to support young peopleHinton is putting his attention into a non-profit initiative called Bounce Back. It aims to give young people opportunities to participate in sports, develop practical life skills and explore higher education and career options.The name has a personal connection to his experience as a youth basketball coach and his wife's work in behavioural healthcare. She supports people dealing with mental health and addiction-related difficulties.Hinton also hopes to use the public interest in his friendship with Dench to draw attention to the challenges faced by ordinary families. Rising living costs have made expenses such as Thanksgiving meals and holiday travel more difficult for many households.Although people around him encourage him to be more active on social media, Hinton prefers to concentrate on activities outside the online world."My friends always tell me, 'Hey, you're an influencer. You should post more. You should let people know what's going on with your life,'" he told CNN.His non-profit plans reflect his interest in helping young people access opportunities that may otherwise seem difficult to reach.Dench takes up activities beyond ThanksgivingDench is also exploring new interests as she approaches her 70th birthday. She has been making friends in her neighbourhood and recently began working with other women on quilts that will be donated to cancer patients.The activity is particularly meaningful to her because she has undergone cancer treatment herself. Remembering how cold chemotherapy sessions could be, she wants to provide something useful to patients going through the experience.Now cancer-free, Dench sees the project as one way of supporting others. She also wants to remain open to new friendships and experiences rather than treating age as a reason to slow down."I'm learning that just because I'm a senior citizen now, it doesn't mean my life is over," she told CNN.She does not have a detailed plan for the years ahead and prefers to see where new opportunities take her."I've just learned in life that you start somewhere and I'm just always amazed on where I end up because it's always a surprise, and so I don't have an exact plan," Dench said.
